svg.text: Bernoulli's equation and its uses, viscous drag, terminal velocity and superfluids

g.text: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant

svg.text: Uses of Bernoulli's principle (5.12, Figs. 5.17 to 5.23)

g.text: 1 aeroplane wing: streamlines closer above the wing, faster air, lower pressure, lift
2 swing of a ball: air faster over the rough side, slower over the smooth side; the
pressure difference gives a sideways force (Magnus effect) and the ball curves
3 filter pump: a constriction speeds the water jet, pressure drops, air is drawn in
4 carburetor: fast air in a Venturi duct has low pressure and draws in petrol vapour
5 paint sprayer, atomizer: air over a tube dipped in liquid lowers the pressure, so
atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up and out of the nozzle
6 Venturi relation: horizontal pipe, P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho (v2^2 - v1^2) (5.25);
with v1 much smaller than v2, P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho v2^2 (5.26): the Venturi meter
7 Torricelli's theorem: tank with orifices A and B, v1 of the surface about zero,
P1 = P2 = atmospheric: v2 = sqrt(2 g (h1 - h2)) (5.27): the speed of efflux equals
that of a ball falling through h1 - h2; viscous losses alter the result somewhat
where the speed is high the pressure is low: P + (1/2) rho v^2 = constant; a venturi mask;
standing near a fast train is dangerous; a chimney draws smoke up by the pressure drop

svg.text: Viscous drag, Stokes' law and terminal velocity (5.13, 5.14)
at terminal velocity the two balance

g.text: F = 6 pi eta r v (5.28), slow speeds only
0 = m g - 6 pi eta r v_t
v_t = m g / (6 pi eta r) (5.30)
m = rho (4/3) pi r^3 -> v_t = 2 g r^2 rho/(9 eta) (5.31)
Example 5.5: fog droplet r = 0.010 cm = 1.0 x 10^-4 m,
viscosity measures the force needed to slide one layer
over another; tar and honey large, water small; drag
grows with speed (hand out of a car window)
viscosities at 30 C (10^-3 N s m^-2): air 0.019, acetone 0.295, methanol 0.510,
benzene 0.564, water 0.801, ethanol 1.000, plasma 1.6, glycerin 6.29

svg.text: parachutes increase air drag with a large surface area, so the fall slows and the landing is safe

g.text: ideal fluid: no viscosity, incompressible (infinite bulk modulus), no surface tension;
exists only in theory. real fluid: has viscosity (kerosene, castor oil, honey, water,
diesel, petrol), compressible to some degree, finite bulk modulus, surface tension
superfluid: zero viscosity, frictionless; flows without loss of kinetic energy; forms
in some substances at cryogenic temperatures near absolute zero; flows through
very narrow spaces and climbs container walls against gravity (film flow, Fig. 5.24)
properties: persistent vortices when stirred; the liquid stays still when its container
rotates; a mixture of normal and superfluid components, more superfluid when colder;
high thermal conductivity; differs from superconductivity (helium-3 and helium-4 do
not conduct electricity)
examples: helium-4 (superfluid a few degrees below its boiling point of -269 C, 4 K),
helium-3, some Bose-Einstein condensates, rubidium-85, lithium-6 at 50 nK, sodium,
possibly inside neutron stars
uses: helium-4 coolant for high-field magnets; both isotopes in particle detectors;
liquid helium in cryogenics, superconducting magnets, leak testing, electronics and optics
